title: CSC3710 2026-09-08 — Set Operations, Languages, and Regular Sets

questions.q: Let X = {a, λ} and Y = {b, λ}. What is XY (simplified)?
questions.explain: Pair every u ∈ X with every v ∈ Y: ab, aλ = a, λb = b, λλ = λ. No two coincide, so XY = {ab, a, b, λ}. Forgetting that λ pairs with things (or treating λ as 'nothing to pair') gives the wrong answers.

questions.q: Let X = {a, ab, λ} and Y = {λ, b, a} (the lecture example). How many elements does XY have?
questions.explain: Nine pairs are formed, but aλ = λa = a and ab·λ = a·b = ab each merge two pairs into one string. 9 − 2 = 7: XY = {a, ab, aa, abb, aba, λ, b}.

questions.q: Let X = {a, ab, λ} and Y = {λ, b, a}. How many elements does X × Y have?
questions.explain: For finite sets |X × Y| = |X| · |Y| = 3 · 3 = 9. Ordered pairs never merge: (a, λ) and (λ, a) are different pairs even though they glue to the same string.

questions.q: Why is |XY| ≤ |X × Y| for finite sets of strings X and Y?
choices: Because different pairs (u, v) can glue into the same string uv, while ordered pairs stay distinct
Because X × Y also contains pairs like (v, u)
questions.explain: The map f(u, v) = uv from X × Y to XY is onto (every string of XY comes from some pair), but different pairs can glue to the same string because the 'seam' disappears. An onto map can't have more outputs than inputs.

questions.q: It is possible to have |XY| < |X| · |Y| even when neither X nor Y contains λ.
questions.explain: Example: X = {a, ab}, Y = {b, bb}. a·bb = abb = ab·b, so XY = {ab, abb, abbb} has 3 < 4 elements. λ is one cause of merging, but overlapping pieces are another.

questions.q: For which pair of sets does |XY| = |X × Y| hold?
questions.explain: {a, b}{a, b} = {aa, ab, ba, bb}: four distinct strings from four pairs. In the others, pairs merge: aλ = λa; a·aa = aa·a; ab·b = a·bb.

questions.q: Which statement correctly contrasts X × Y and XY?
choices: X × Y contains ordered pairs (u, v); XY contains single strings uv
Both contain strings, but X × Y keeps duplicates
X × Y is always smaller than XY
They are the same set written with different symbols
questions.explain: The Cartesian product builds ordered pairs whose parts can always be recovered; concatenation glues the parts into one string, losing the boundary.

questions.q: Let X = {a, ba} and Y = {λ, a}. Which strings are in XY?
questions.explain: The pairs give aλ = a, aa, baλ = ba, baa. All four are distinct, so |XY| = 4 = |X × Y|. ab would need b to come first from Y, which is impossible.

questions.q: When simplifying XY, the strings ab and ba can be merged into one element because they use the same symbols.
questions.explain: Strings are sequences: order matters, so ab ≠ ba and both are kept. Only identical strings (like aλ and λa, both equal to a) collapse.

questions.q: Set concatenation is commutative: XY = YX for all sets of strings X and Y.
questions.explain: Counterexample: {a}{b} = {ab} but {b}{a} = {ba}. XY = YX holds for some special sets (e.g. Y = ∅ or Y = {λ}), but that doesn't make the operation commutative.

questions.q: For all sets of strings X, Y, Z: (XY)Z = X(YZ).
questions.explain: Both sets consist of strings uvw with u ∈ X, v ∈ Y, w ∈ Z, because string concatenation is associative: (uv)w = u(vw). So we can write XYZ without parentheses.

questions.q: What is X∅ for a nonempty set of strings X?
questions.explain: A string of X∅ needs a second part from ∅, and ∅ offers none, so no string can be formed. ∅ absorbs concatenation like 0 absorbs multiplication. Answering X confuses ∅ with {λ}.

questions.q: What is {λ}X?
questions.explain: The only possible first part is λ, and λw = w, so every string of X comes out unchanged. {λ} is the identity for concatenation, like 1 for multiplication.

questions.q: In the analogy between set concatenation and multiplication of numbers, which sets play the roles of 0 and 1?
questions.explain: ∅ absorbs (X∅ = ∅, like x · 0 = 0) and {λ} is the identity (X{λ} = X, like x · 1 = x).

questions.q: For which of these choices does XY = YX hold? (X, Y sets of strings over {a, b} unless stated.)
questions.explain: Y = ∅ gives ∅ both ways; Y = {λ} gives X both ways; powers of one set commute (XᵐXⁿ = X^(m+n)); over a one-symbol alphabet every string is aᵏ and aⁱaʲ = aʲaⁱ. X = {a}, Y = {b} fails: {ab} ≠ {ba}.

questions.q: Because X{λ} = {λ}X for every X, we may conclude that set concatenation is commutative.
questions.explain: A property like commutativity must hold for all X and Y. One special partner ({λ}, or ∅) commuting with everything is not enough; {a}{b} ≠ {b}{a} is a counterexample.

questions.q: A student writes {ab, b}∅ = {ab, b}. What is the mistake?
choices: They confused ∅ with {λ}; the answer is ∅
The answer should be {ab, b, λ}
questions.explain: They treated ∅ like {λ}. {ab, b}{λ} = {ab, b}, but {ab, b}∅ = ∅ because ∅ provides no string to put second.

questions.q: In the recursive definition of Xⁿ, what is X⁰?
questions.explain: X⁰ = {λ}, the identity for concatenation, just as x⁰ = 1. With ∅ as the basis, every power would be ∅ (since ∅X = ∅).

questions.q: Which is the recursive step of the definition of powers?
questions.explain: Xᵏ = Xᵏ⁻¹X for k ≥ 1: each power is the previous power concatenated with X once more.

questions.q: For Σ = {a, b}, what is Σ²?
questions.explain: Σ² = Σ¹Σ = {a, b}{a, b} = {aa, ab, ba, bb}: all strings of length 2. ab and ba are both present because order matters.

questions.q: In words, Σⁿ is the set of all strings over Σ of length ___. (fill in)
questions.explain: Each concatenation with Σ adds exactly one symbol, starting from λ (length 0), so Σⁿ contains exactly the strings of length n.

questions.q: For Σ = {a, b, c}, how many elements does Σ³ have?
questions.explain: Each of the 3 positions can hold any of 3 symbols: |Σⁿ| = |Σ|ⁿ = 3³ = 27.

questions.q: For Σ = {a, b}, how many elements does Σ⁰ have?
questions.explain: Σ⁰ = {λ}, which has one element (the empty string). It is not empty — consistent with 2⁰ = 1.

questions.q: Using the recursive definition, what is X¹ and why?
questions.explain: X¹ = X⁰X = {λ}X = X, since {λ} is the identity. This matches 5¹ = 5 for numbers.

questions.q: What is {a, bb}²?
questions.explain: {a, bb}{a, bb} = {a·a, a·bb, bb·a, bb·bb} = {aa, abb, bba, bbbb}.

questions.q: All strings in {a, bb}³ have the same length.
questions.explain: The pieces have different lengths (1 and 2), so three pieces give lengths 3 (aaa) through 6 (bbbbbb). Only when every piece has the same length (like Σ) do all strings of Xⁿ share a length.

questions.q: How many elements does {a, bb}³ have?
questions.explain: Each of 3 positions picks a or bb: 2³ = 8 sequences, and here no two sequences give the same string (aaa, aabb, abba, abbbb, bbaa, bbabb, bbbba, bbbbbb).

questions.q: Which expression defines the Kleene star X\*?
questions.explain: X\* = X⁰ ∪ X¹ ∪ X² ∪ …: concatenations of zero or more strings of X, with repetition. The i = 0 term contributes λ.

questions.q: λ ∈ X\* for every set of strings X, including X = ∅.
questions.explain: X\* always includes X⁰ = {λ}, whatever X is. So even ∅\* = {λ}.

questions.q: Which is a correct definition of the positive closure X⁺?
questions.explain: X⁺ = XX\* (= X\*X = X¹ ∪ X² ∪ …): one or more strings of X concatenated.

questions.q: For Σ = {a, b}, what is Σ\*Σ?
choices: Σ⁺, all nonempty strings over {a, b}
questions.explain: Every string of Σ\*Σ ends with the symbol contributed by the final Σ, so λ is excluded; every nonempty string w splits as (w minus last symbol)(last symbol), so all nonempty strings are included: Σ\*Σ = Σ⁺ = Σ\* − {λ}.

questions.q: Which identities hold for every set of strings X?
questions.explain: X\* = X⁺ ∪ {λ} (the star is the plus with the i = 0 term added), and XX\* = X\*X = X⁺. X⁺ = X\* − {λ} fails when λ ∈ X (then λ ∈ X⁺). X\* = X ∪ {λ} fails whenever X has a nonempty string (ww is missing).

questions.q: Exactly when is λ ∈ X⁺?
questions.explain: If λ ∈ X then λ ∈ X¹ ⊆ X⁺. If λ ∉ X, each string of X has length ≥ 1, so each string of Xⁱ (i ≥ 1) has length ≥ i ≥ 1, and λ ∉ X⁺. 'Plus means no λ' is only true when λ ∉ X.

questions.q: Let X = {λ, ab}. Which is true?
questions.explain: λ ∈ X, so λ ∈ X⁺, and X⁺ = X⁺ ∪ {λ} = X\*. Both equal {λ, ab, abab, …}.

questions.q: Let Y = {ab}. Which is true?
questions.explain: λ ∉ Y, so every string of Y⁺ has length ≥ 2: Y⁺ = {ab, abab, …} while Y\* = {λ, ab, abab, …}. They differ only by λ.

questions.q: The superscript ⁺ is read as "one or ___". (fill in one word)
questions.explain: X⁺ is concatenations of one or more strings of X, versus X\*, zero or more.

questions.q: If X contains at least one nonempty string, then X\* is infinite.
questions.explain: If w ≠ λ is in X, then w, ww, www, … are all in X\* and have strictly increasing lengths, so they are all distinct.

questions.q: Which list gives the shortest elements of {a, b}\* in order?
choices: a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, …
λ, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, …
questions.explain: {a,b}\* = {λ} ∪ {a, b} ∪ {aa, ab, ba, bb} ∪ … — it starts with λ, which comes from Σ⁰.

questions.q: What is ∅\*?
questions.explain: ∅\* = ∅⁰ ∪ ∅¹ ∪ … . ∅⁰ = {λ} (any set to the 0 is {λ}), and ∅ⁿ = ∅ⁿ⁻¹∅ = ∅ for n ≥ 1. So ∅\* = {λ}.

questions.q: What is {λ}\*?
questions.explain: Every power of {λ} is {λ}, since {λ}{λ} = {λλ} = {λ}. The union of copies of {λ} is {λ}.

questions.q: What is ∅⁺?
questions.explain: ∅⁺ = ∅∅\* = ∅{λ} = ∅. Consistent with 'λ ∈ X⁺ iff λ ∈ X': λ ∉ ∅.

questions.q: What is {λ}⁺?
questions.explain: {λ}⁺ = {λ}{λ}\* = {λ}{λ} = {λ}. Here λ ∈ X, so λ ∈ X⁺.

questions.q: For which sets X is X\* finite?
questions.explain: Only ∅ and {λ} have finite stars (both give {λ}). Any set containing a nonempty string w yields w, ww, www, … — infinitely many strings.

questions.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes λ, {λ} and ∅?
choices: They are three names for the same thing
λ and ∅ are the same; {λ} is different
λ is a string of length 0; {λ} is a set with one element; ∅ is a set with zero elements
questions.explain: λ is a string (not a set); {λ} is a set with one element, λ; ∅ has no elements at all. As concatenation partners, {λ} is the identity and ∅ absorbs.

questions.q: How many elements does the set {λ} have?
questions.explain: One: the empty string. The string has length 0, but the set has one element. Contrast |∅| = 0.
By the basis of the definition of powers, X⁰ = {λ} for every X, including ∅. That's why ∅\* contains λ.

questions.q: The lecture compared checking a definition on ∅ and {λ} to unit-testing a function meant for natural numbers. Which inputs correspond to the 'boundary' test?
choices: The edge value 0 (and, for definitions, ∅ and {λ})
questions.explain: Test a typical value (5), the boundary value (0) and an invalid one (−5). ∅ and {λ} are the 'special sets' — every other set we use contains a string with at least one symbol — so a definition should be checked on them.

questions.q: Which is the recursive step in the recursive definition of Σ\*?
choices: If w ∈ Σ\* and a ∈ Σ, then wa ∈ Σ\*
If w ∈ Σ\*, then ww ∈ Σ\*
If a ∈ Σ, then a ∈ Σ\*
If w ∈ Σ\*, then w\* ∈ Σ\*
questions.explain: Basis: λ ∈ Σ\*. Recursive step: if w ∈ Σ\* and a ∈ Σ, then wa ∈ Σ\*. Closure: only strings reachable from λ in finitely many steps. (w is a string, a is a symbol, following the naming convention.)

questions.q: What is the basis of the recursive definition of Σ\*?
choices: Every a ∈ Σ is in Σ\*
questions.explain: The only basis element is λ. Single symbols are then obtained in one step: λa = a.

questions.q: Using the recursive definition of Σ\* (Σ = {a, b}), how many applications of the recursive step are needed to show bab ∈ Σ\*, starting from the basis?
questions.explain: λ → b (w = λ, symbol b) → ba (w = b, symbol a) → bab (w = ba, symbol b). One step per symbol, so 3.

questions.q: What does the closure clause of a recursive definition (like that of Σ\*) accomplish?
choices: It says the set is closed under union
It excludes everything not reachable from the basis in finitely many steps
It adds infinite strings as limits
questions.explain: The basis and recursive step only say what is IN. The closure clause says nothing else is: the set is the smallest one satisfying the rules, containing only objects reached in finitely many steps. That's why every element of Σ\* is finite and why structural induction works.

questions.q: A language over an alphabet Σ is…
choices: any infinite set of strings over Σ
questions.explain: By definition, any subset of Σ\* — no requirement of being infinite, nonempty, or interesting.

questions.q: Let Σ = {a, b}. Which of these are languages over Σ?
questions.explain: Check L ⊆ Σ\*. Σ\* ⊆ Σ\*; ∅ is a subset of every set; λ ∈ Σ\* (the basis), so {λ} ⊆ Σ\*; aba, bbb ∈ Σ\*. But c ∉ Σ, so {ab, c} ⊄ Σ\* (it is a language over {a, b, c}).

questions.q: ∅ is not a language because it contains no strings.
questions.explain: ∅ ⊆ Σ\*, so it meets the definition. It is a set of strings that happens to contain none — a real, if uninteresting, language. This was a wrong answer corrected in class.

questions.q: ∅ and {λ} are the same language.
questions.explain: ∅ has no strings; {λ} has exactly one, the empty string. They're different languages.

questions.q: When English is modeled as a formal language whose alphabet is the set of English words, what is a sentence?
choices: A string over the alphabet of words
questions.explain: Each word is one indivisible symbol, so a sentence is a finite sequence of symbols — a string over that alphabet — and English is a particular set of such strings.

questions.q: The alphabet of words for a language like Java can be treated as finite, even though there are very many possible identifiers.
questions.explain: An alphabet must be finite. Identifiers follow rules and are bounded in length in practice, so the set of possible 'words' is huge but finite.

questions.q: In the course's naming convention, what do letters like a, b, c and u, v, w denote?
choices: a, b, c are strings; u, v, w are symbols
a, b, c are symbols; u, v, w are strings
a, b, c are sets; u, v, w are languages
questions.explain: Letters from the start of the alphabet are symbols; letters from the end are strings. So in 'w ∈ Σ\*, a ∈ Σ ⇒ wa ∈ Σ\*', w is a string and a a symbol.

questions.q: Over Σ = {a, b}, the set of all languages is P(Σ\*). How big is it?
questions.explain: Σ\* is countably infinite (list in shortlex order). By Cantor's theorem the power set of a countably infinite set is uncountable. Since regular expressions, DFAs and Turing machines are finite strings, there are only countably many of each — so most languages aren't regular, or even recognizable.

questions.q: Why is Σ\* (for finite Σ) countable?
choices: Its strings can be listed by length, then alphabetically, and each appears at a finite position
Its strings can be listed in plain dictionary order
questions.explain: In shortlex order — by length, then alphabetically — λ, a, b, aa, ab, ba, bb, aaa, … every string appears at some finite position, giving a correspondence with ℕ. Pure alphabetical order fails: a, aa, aaa, … never reaches b.

questions.q: Over Σ = {a, b}, which sets are basis elements of the regular sets?
questions.explain: The basis is ∅, {λ}, and {x} for each symbol x ∈ Σ — here exactly four sets. {a, b} is regular but not basic: it is built as {a} ∪ {b}.

questions.q: Which operations appear in the recursive step of the definition of regular sets?
questions.explain: Only union, concatenation and Kleene star. Theory says these three suffice for every regular set; practical-regex conveniences like ⁺ or {n} are shorthand for them.

questions.q: Which sequence correctly proves {ab, bb}\* is regular?
questions.explain: {a}, {b} are basis; their union is {a, b}; concatenating with {b} gives {ab, bb}; the star gives {ab, bb}\*. Each step applies one rule to sets already known regular.

questions.q: Which strings are the elements of {ab, bb}\* of length at most 4?
choices: ab, bb, abab, abbb, bbab, bbbb
λ, ab, bb, abab, abbb, bbab, bbbb
questions.explain: Length 0: λ (zero blocks). Length 2: ab, bb. Length 4: all four two-block products abab, abbb, bbab, bbbb. No odd lengths are possible.

questions.q: Which strings are in {ab, bb}\*?
questions.explain: Split into consecutive length-2 blocks and check each is ab or bb: λ (0 blocks), bbab = bb·ab, abbbab = ab·bb·ab. aab has odd length; ba is not a block.

questions.q: Each application of the recursive step in the definition of regular sets produces a new set not obtained before.
questions.explain: It can return an existing set: ∅\* = {λ}, {λ}{λ} = {λ}. That's why the definition says 'are regular sets', not 'new regular sets'.

questions.q: Which description is equivalent to {ab, bb}\*?
choices: Strings that contain ab or bb
Strings of even length in which every symbol in an even position (2nd, 4th, …) is b
questions.explain: Every block has length 2 and ends in b, so strings have even length with b in every even position; conversely such a string splits into pairs of the form ?b, i.e. ab or bb. 'Contains ab' would admit aab, which isn't in the set.

questions.q: What counts as a proof that a set is regular, according to the recursive definition?
choices: Showing it is a subset of Σ\*
A finite sequence of steps from basis sets, each applying ∪, concatenation or \*
questions.explain: The closure clause says a set is regular only if it's obtained from the basis by finitely many recursive steps — so exhibiting such a finite construction proves regularity.

questions.q: In a construction of {ba, bb}\* from the basis, which step directly produces {ba, bb}?
questions.explain: After forming {a, b} = {a} ∪ {b}, concatenate {b} in front: {b}{a, b} = {ba, bb}. Order matters: {a, b}{b} = {ab, bb} is a different set.

questions.q: Every pattern accepted by a modern programming-language regex engine describes a regular set.
questions.explain: Backreferences such as `(a|b)+\1` describe { ww | w ∈ Σ⁺ }, which is provably not regular. Conveniences like `a{10}`, `a+`, `a?`, `[ab]` are just shorthand for the three core operations, but backreferences go beyond them.

questions.q: Over Σ = {a, b}, which core-operation expression matches the practical regex `a{2,4}`?
questions.explain: `a{2,4}` means 2, 3 or 4 a's: the union aa ∪ aaa ∪ aaaa. It only needs union and concatenation.

questions.q: Which of these sets over {a, b} are regular (i.e. can be built from the basis with ∪, concatenation, \*)?
questions.explain: Every finite set is regular (union of concatenations of symbols); {a, b}\*{a} and {a}\*{b}\* are direct constructions; Σ\* = ({a} ∪ {b})\*. { ww | w ∈ Σ⁺ } is the language of backreference-style 'square' strings, which is provably not regular.

questions.q: Describe {aa, ab, ba, bb}\* over {a, b}.
choices: Strings of even length, including λ
Strings of even length, excluding λ
questions.explain: The blocks are all of Σ², so k blocks give length 2k; conversely every even-length string splits into pairs. λ is included (length 0 is even). Say 'even length', not 'even strings'.

questions.q: Describe {a, b}\*{a}.
questions.explain: Any string (possibly λ) followed by a: exactly the strings ending with a. The shortest is λa = a. 'Contains an a' is too broad (ab contains a but doesn't end with it).

questions.q: Describe {b}{a, b}\*.
choices: Strings that start with b, or λ
questions.explain: A leading b followed by any string. λ is not included: every element has the leading b.

questions.q: Describe {a, b}\*{aa}{a, b}\*.
choices: a or b, followed by aa, followed by a or b
Strings that contain aa as a substring
questions.explain: w = x·aa·y for some strings x, y exactly when aa occurs somewhere in w. The stars allow any prefix and suffix, including λ, so the shortest element is aa.

questions.q: A classmate describes {a, b}\*{aa}{a, b}\* as "a or b, followed by aa, followed by a or b". Which set does their description actually match?
questions.explain: They dropped the stars, reading {a, b}\* as {a, b}. That gives {a, b}{aa}{a, b} = {aaaa, aaab, baaa, baab}, a finite set — whereas the starred set is infinite.

questions.q: What is the shortest string in {a, b}\*{aa}{a, b}\*?
questions.explain: Each {a, b}\* factor may contribute λ: λ·aa·λ = aa.

questions.q: Which length-3 strings are in {a, b}\*{aa}{a, b}\*?
questions.explain: The length-3 strings containing aa are aaa, aab, baa. aba and bab do not contain aa.
{a}\*{b}\* is any number of a's followed by any number of b's; order matters, so no a can follow a b. 'Strings of a's and b's' is an imprecise description of it.

questions.q: Describe {a, b}{a, b}\* over {a, b}.
choices: All strings over {a, b}, including λ
questions.explain: One symbol followed by any string: every nonempty string, i.e. Σ⁺. λ is excluded because at least one symbol is forced.

questions.q: What is the recommended method for understanding a set expression?
choices: Convert it to a Cartesian product
List the shortest elements, find the pattern, and state it precisely (including whether λ is in the set)
questions.explain: List the shortest elements, look for the pattern, then state it precisely — including whether λ is in the set.

questions.q: Describe {a, b}\*{bb}{a, b}\*.
choices: Strings that contain the substring bb
Strings that start and end with b
Strings with at least two b's
questions.explain: Same shape as Example D with bb in place of aa: any prefix, then bb, then any suffix.

questions.q: "Strings with at least two b's" is a precise description of {a, b}\*{bb}{a, b}\*.
questions.explain: bab has two b's but no substring bb, so it's not in the set. The b's must be adjacent: 'contains the substring bb'.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: Which regular expression (course notation) denotes {a, b}\*{aa}{a, b}\*?
questions.explain: {a, b} = {a} ∪ {b} becomes (a ∪ b); concatenation is juxtaposition; the star carries over.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: Which regular expression denotes the strings over {a, b} that start with a?
questions.explain: Force a first, then any string: a(a ∪ b)\*. (a ∪ b)\*a is 'ends with a'; a\* includes λ and misses ab; a(a ∪ b) has length exactly 2.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: Which regular expressions denote the strings over {a, b} of even length?
questions.explain: Repeat a length-2 block zero or more times: ((a ∪ b)(a ∪ b))\* or (aa ∪ ab ∪ ba ∪ bb)\*. (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)\* is all nonempty strings; (ab ∪ bb)\* misses aa.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: Which regular expression denotes the strings over {a, b} that contain the substring bab?
questions.explain: Any prefix, then bab, then any suffix. (ba ∪ b)\* doesn't force bab; bab\* means ba followed by b's.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: With standard precedence, how is ab\* ∪ c read?
questions.explain: Star binds tightest, then concatenation, then union: (a(b\*)) ∪ c.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: Which of these denote the same set as (a ∪ b)\*aa(a ∪ b)\*, depending on the source's notation?
questions.explain: Union is written ∪ (Sudkamp/this course), + (many textbooks) or | (programming regex and most online tools). Beware: in programming regex, + means 'one or more'.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: What is the relationship between regular expressions and regular sets?
choices: A regular expression is a compact notation denoting a regular set
Regular sets are a notation for regular expressions
Every set of strings has a regular expression
questions.explain: Regular expressions are abbreviations for regular sets, mirroring the definition clause by clause: ∅, λ, a, union, concatenation, star.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: Two regular expressions are called equivalent when…
choices: one can be obtained by removing parentheses from the other
questions.explain: Equivalence means they denote the same set of strings, even if written differently.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: In the online equivalence checker, what does leaving an input field empty mean?
questions.explain: An empty field is λ, the regular expression for {λ}. (Union is typed as |.)

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: You compare `(a|b)*` with an empty field in the checker. What does it report?
choices: Accepted by first but not second: a
Accepted by second but not first: λ
Accepted by first but not second: λ
questions.explain: Both sets contain λ, so λ isn't a difference. The shortest string in the first but not {λ} is a (first alphabetically among length 1).

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: You compare `(a|b)*aa(a|b)*` with an empty field. What does the checker report?
choices: Only: accepted by first but not second: aa
Only: accepted by second but not first: λ
questions.explain: λ is in {λ} but not in Example D (every element contains aa), and aa is the shortest string of Example D, which isn't in {λ}.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: You compare `(a|b)*b` with `(a|b)*`. What does the checker report?
choices: Accepted by second but not first: λ
Accepted by first but not second: b
Accepted by second but not first: a
questions.explain: Every string ending in b is in (a|b)\*, so nothing is in the first but not the second. The shortest string of (a|b)\* that doesn't end in b is λ.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: How can the checker be used to discover the members of a set, shortest first?
choices: Enter Σ\* as the second expression
Put the strings found so far in the second expression and read off the next reported difference
questions.explain: Each report is the shortest difference. Add each string found to the second expression (aa, then aa|aaa, …) and the tool reveals the next shortest member each time.

questions.category: Regular expressions and the equivalence checker
questions.q: Which pairs of regular expressions over {a, b} are equivalent?
questions.explain: (a ∪ b)\* and (a\*b\*)\* both give every string (a\*b\* includes a and b, so its star contains everything). (a ∪ b)(a ∪ b)\* and (a ∪ b)\*(a ∪ b) are both Σ⁺. a\*b\* ≠ (ab)\*: a is in the first, not the second. (ab ∪ λ)\* = (ab)\*, since adding λ to a set doesn't change its star.
